subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT OF ONTARIO-APPOINTMENT OF SIX WOMEN MINISTERS
speechtext: Today in this House, Mr. Speaker, I should like to extend my congratulations to the Government of Ontario, and particularly to Premier David Peterson. Thirty new Ministers were sworn in yesterday, including six women: Mrs. Lily Munro, Mrs. Elinor Caplan, Mrs. Joan Smith, Mrs. Chaviva Hosek, Mrs. Lyn McLeod, and Mrs. Mavis Wilson.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT OF ONTARIO-APPOINTMENT OF SIX WOMEN MINISTERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT OF ONTARIO-APPOINTMENT OF SIX WOMEN MINISTERS
speechtext:
Of sixteen elected women, six were appointed to Cabinet, telling evidence of the Government's political will to promote equality.
I should like to mention that Mrs. Chaviva Hosek was given the housing portfolio. I remind the House that Mrs. Hosek has shown leadershsip in causes of women and minorities. We are very pleased that her new duties are recognition she deserves.
To Mrs. Hosek and all her female Ontario Cabinet colleagues we say: Bravo!

Bravo! Hang in there. You are a vital role model and there will be more to come.

subsubtopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY STRIKE BY MARINE ENGINEERS- REQUEST THAT MINISTER INTERVENE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, work stoppage along the St. Lawrence Seaway, initiated by the Canadian Marine Officers Union, is of great concern to the people of Saskatchewan. Withdrawal of services by engineers
threatens grain ships on the St. Lawrence Seaway and could possibly halt 75 per cent of all shipping.
Saskatchewan farmers are finishing their harvesting and want to begin quickly moving their grains through the transportation system. Saskatchewan is already feeling the negative effects of the engineering strike, namely, the rail limits on wheat transportation recently imposed in our province. This is unacceptable to the people of Saskatchewan who must meet marketing quotas.
The devastating effects of another transportation disruption could severely cripple the economies of Saskatchewan and its neighbouring provinces. Put simply, Mr. Speaker, the western economy will not be able to endure another marketing delay. For this reason I call on my hon. colleague, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux), to intervene in the collective bargaining process to ensure that an agreement is reached quickly and that the interests of farmers across Canada are protected.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF FIRST ELECTION OF SPEAKER
ANNIVERSARY OF FIRST ELECTION OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to the attention of the House that it was one year ago today that we as Members of Parliament opened a new chapter in the evolution of the practices and traditions of the House of Commons with the first ever election of a Speaker.

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF FIRST ELECTION OF SPEAKER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: ANNIVERSARY OF FIRST ELECTION OF SPEAKER
speechtext:
Members will recall that the McGrath Special Committee on Parliamentary Reform first addressed the idea of an elected Speaker. It was to the credit of all parties that this progressive and historic increase in the influence of the Members of the House was made.
The election process was long and somewhat cumbersome, as the democratic process often is, but the excellent choice that we made on that historic night has demonstrated that this new procedure serves Members well.
I am certain that I speak for all Members of the House, Mr. Speaker, when I say that you have served Parliament and Canada well over the past year. Your decisions have been thoughtful and fair. The obvious respect that Members have

September 30, 1987
for you has brought a renewed atmosphere of civility, dignity, and respect to this House.
This is a place where great issues of the day are raised and debated, where passions run high, and where patience is put to the test. It is a rare individual indeed who can preside over such a place and enforce the rules and procedures with the great care and skill which ensure that the rights and privileges of all Members are respected.
In you, Mr. Speaker, we have found such a rare individual. We look forward to continuing to work with you in the months and years ahead.
[Editor's Note: Whereupon all Hon. Members rose and applauded.]

On November 4, 1986, Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) introduced in the House Bill C-18 to set the needed legislative framework to ease the economic control over the Canadian transportation industry.
Our Government had put forward measures to enhance competition and greater market force freeplay, so that Canadian users could benefit from more competitive prices and a greater service choice.
Mr. Speaker, this Bill was given Royal Assent less than a month ago and its positive effects are already being felt.
For instance, Air Alma Incorporated, an airline operating in my riding, has been offering since Monday a new service to its travelling customers thanks to Bill C-18 and this, to the delight of the regional population who will have at its disposal two more flights every day to travel to the capital city of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-18 is only one of a great many initiatives of our Government which are beneficial to our regions.

Mr. Speaker, although initially I was one of those who accepted reluctantly your nomination today I must admit I was wrong and I congratulate you.
This being said, I was pleased yesterday, to meet with representatives of the Montreal Harbour employees, and those 1,000 workers proved to us that the accident rate in Montreal Harbour is much higher than anywhere else in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the stated causes of such a high accident level were: first, working hours are too long because dock workers are required, or forced to work between 60 and 80 hours a week. Second, absolutely no workers safety program. Third, no equipment inspection in Montreal Harbour.
Mr. Speaker, I urge the Minister of State (Transport) to meet within the shortest time frame with representatives of the Montreal Harbour employees, in order to force Montreal Harbour and all Canadian harbours to have work safety as their first priority, otherwise there will be a serious conflict in Montreal.

subsubtopic: POSTAL STRIKE-SUGGESTION POSTAL SERVICE BE DECLARED ESSENTIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Post Office is on strike again. So, what else is new?
This country cannot be held at ransom again by CUPW, who, according to press reports, state that they are concerned about violence on the picket lines.
Shirley Carr of the CLC says that she is afraid that someone will be killed on the lines this time around.
I do not dispute that people have the right to strike, but I find it hard to believe that, in Canada, CUPW can threaten and intimidate those who are willing to work at the Post Office and accept their terms of employment.
The Post Office is an essential service and when it is on strike there are too many innocent victims, including small businesses, seniors, the disabled, and indeed all Canadians. As regrettable as I feel this action is, perhaps it is time to consider declaring Canada Post an essential service and removing the right to strike.
September 30, 1987

subsubtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-TREATMENT OF BLACK CHILDREN-WORLD REACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the children of South Africa are going to a special school today. It is a school of the real world.
They are learning that brutal tyranny and the ruthless subjugation of a people do not mobilize nations as much as they mobilize words. Some are noble words, promising action, like those of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Some are the transparent words, like those who would use guns to defend English sheep on a far off island that cannot be her own. Some are the words of collaborators sent abroad to earn their keep from the oppressor. And there are the influential words of those not cured of latent racism, the mendacious Minister turned columnist, the retired judge, and the official spokesman of those who would keep Canada pure and, being consistent, spit calumny upon the victims of racism in South Africa.
Will we take home a lesson for the black children of South Africa, the fulfilled promise of the Prime Minister, or must they foresee that the negative voices will be the more compelling and that they should look elsewhere if ever they are to achieve freedom?

subsubtopic: UNITED STATES CONGRESSIONAL COMMITTEE'S STUDY OF PROPOSED NEW DOLLAR COIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, copying being the sincerest form of flattery, it is interesting to note that a committee of members of the American House of Representatives and Senate is proposing that the United States mint a gold coloured one dollar coin.
The success of the Canadian gold "looney" vis-a-vis the silver Susan B. Anthony has evidently done much to prompt this reconsideration.
In order to retain the compatibility between Canadian and U.S. coinage, it would be advantageous for the Americans to adopt size and weight specifications similar to ours. We could help them with the special technology needed to coat the nickel blanks which we could also supply to them should they so wish.
The Royal Canadian Mint must be proud of its successful coinage innovations which other countries look to as a source of inspiration.

Mr. Speaker, there is a new wrinkle in the ongoing saga of "close encounters of the capital kind". The "capital kind encounters" we are talking about are the parties that will be taking place tonight in various homes across the City of Ottawa.
There have been a number of suggestions that these parties have been set up to lobby. However, according to the exConservative Member of Parliament who says these are not lobbying parties: "If anyone comes to try to sell them submarines, staplers, or whiskey, this is the wrong place to do it. They are probably-" the Ministers "-just going to be looking for pretty girls".
Given that Mr. Binks is hosting a party tonight where the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) will be present, I am quite sure that the Hon. Minister would not accept an invitation to a party where he is going just to look for pretty girls.
I am sure that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in protest at the comments that have been made by his soon-to-be host, Mr. Binks, will decline the invitation and boycott the party tonight so he can put an end to these "close encounters of the capital kind".

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL CONCERNING DUMP AT CANTLEY IN QUEBEC

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO BEN JOHNSON, WORLD CHAMPION SPRINTER
TRIBUTE TO BEN JOHNSON, WORLD CHAMPION SPRINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the realities of this House is that the rhetoric of parliamentary debate tends to draw members into the use of superlatives more often than they should. The biggest and best all too often turn out to be not quite so large and, frankly, not that good.
There is one superlative I want to use today about which there is no question, that is, the fastest. It applies to Canada's Ben Johnson, the fastest human being in the world.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO BEN JOHNSON, WORLD CHAMPION SPRINTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO BEN JOHNSON, WORLD CHAMPION SPRINTER
speechtext:
Just a little while ago, Mr. Speaker, Ben Johnson lined up against the world's best sprinters and left them in his dust as he shattered the world record for the 100-metre dash. He covered the distance in only 9.83 seconds, shaving a full tenth of a second off the old record.
Ben is now back in Canada to receive the credit and the praise that he so justly deserves. He has carried his success with grace and with style.
I ask all members to join with me in congratulating Ben as he visits Parliament Hill today and to express our best wishes and our confidence in him for many future successes.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO BEN JOHNSON, WORLD CHAMPION SPRINTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO BEN JOHNSON, WORLD CHAMPION SPRINTER
speechtext: I can say to our distinguished guest, Mr. Johnson, that while he was scheduled to be on the program a few minutes from now, the demonstration of affection and admiration that has been given to him is timely, is very sincere, and is very warmly meant.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO BEN JOHNSON, WORLD CHAMPION SPRINTER
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, they have done it to us again. For the second time in less than three months the powerful Canadian Union of Postal Workers is holding our country at ransom in an attempt to accomplish their own selfish goals.
Carefully planned rotating strikes, occurred in Victoria and Montreal today.
I have received calls from my constituents in Kootenay East-Revelstoke pleading for quick action to be taken by the Government. From our elderly citizens who are counting on monthly support payments to the businesses which demand a
reliable postal service, we will all suffer the effects of this totally irresponsible and selfish act by the postal union.
Unions should not be allowed the freedom to disrupt a vital national service such as the Post Office. This action will only place undue hardship on innocent Canadians. The disruptive action taken by this union cannot and should not be tolerated. I strongly urge our Government to take decisive and immediate action to release the strangle-hold this national union has on our citizens.

subsubtopic: SEVENTIETH ANNIVERSARY OF ALLIED JEWISH COMMUNITIES SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last Allied Jewish Communities Services held its 70th annual meeting and accounted for its stewardship of the 17 affiliated social educational and cultural institutions which guide, enable, and promote the interests and concerns of the Jewish community of Montreal.
Over 1,600 people attended, bore witness and paid tribute to the volunteer and professional leadership which has enabled the communal service organization to reflect the heart and soul of this very heterogeneous society.
From 1762 on Jews have made their home, and have become part of the fabric of the Canadian and Quebec society. Successive waves of immigrants, seeking safe harbour from discrimination or economic hardship, have come to Canadian shores, speaking a myriad of languages and reflecting diverse cultures.
We have become a bilingual, multicultural and yet highly identifiable minority in Quebec and in Canada. I salute AJCS on its 70th birthday for its enriching contribution to the development of outstanding leaders, both communal and civic, in all areas of life of our people in Canada, in Quebec and, in particular, in Montreal.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister for International Trade said last night that there has been some movement in the American position on free trade. Canadians would be interested in knowing about that. They would be even more interested in knowing whether there has been any Canadian movement on its position in the negotiations with the United States, particularly on the issues of subsidies and our culture.
The Government has virtually destroyed the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. It has weakened the whole issue of regional subsidies. The Government has already sold most of our book publishing industry to the Americans and yielded and withdrawn, apparently, a film distribution policy in the face of American pressure.
What movement has there been on the part of the Americans? And what concessions has Canada been prepared to make by way of a counter proposal?

Mr. Speaker, in regard to the comments of my right hon. friend, the quite careless comments about regional economic expansion, I would point out to him something that he cares to neglect, that in all regions of the country, particularly those far removed from the centre, there has been a decrease in unemployment since this Government came to office, in all of the regions of this country, relative to the figures that were in place on September 17, 1984.
The 907,000 new jobs created in Canada is an important figure. The OECD report indicating that Canada's economy is growing at the top rate of all 24 members of the OECD is, 1 think, an important reflection of what we have been trying to do for the last three years as well. Trade, of course, is an important component of that, in all of its facets.
The Minister for International Trade indicated quite properly that there had been some movement on the important principle of dispute settlement. There has not been, however, agreement on the rules that might govern this mechanism. This is what is presently being considered. If, at an appropriate time, we receive an acceptable response from the Americans in this important area, I will be happy to advise my right hon. friend.
Oral Questions

subtopic: ISSUE OF MECHANISM TO SETTLE CANADIAN-AMERICAN DISPUTES-GOVERNMENT POSITION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: ISSUE OF MECHANISM TO SETTLE CANADIAN-AMERICAN DISPUTES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, such sectors as culture and regional grants contribute to the definition of Canada's very essence, and I believe that Canadians ought to know the position of the Government of Canada in these negotiations. The Prime Minister indicated there has been some movement with respect to the matter of a dispute settlement mechanism between both countries.
Can the Prime Minister tell the House whether his Government continues to insist, as do most Members of the House, that such a mechanism be binding and coupled with a significant exemption from the United States' unilateral right to slap countervailing duties and taxes on Canadian exports?

subtopic: ISSUE OF MECHANISM TO SETTLE CANADIAN-AMERICAN DISPUTES-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the initiatives we took in Northern Ontario, in Western Canada and, more recently, in the Atlantic region- commitments in excess of $1 billion-indicate to what extent the Government is intent on minimizing regional disparities. That is one of the major thrusts of the Government's national policy.
As to the second point raised by my Hon. friend concerning the mechanism, yes, we feel it is an important mechanism to settle disputes which might break out between our two countries as a result of the possible implementation of a free trade agreement. It seems normal to us that an impartial mechanism be available to enable both parties to settle their own disputes, should these occur after the possible negotiation of a more comprehensive agreement. This is the position I had announced practically from the outset, and our current efforts to achieve it attest to unfailing consistency on our part.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry would keep his preamble to the facts needed to place his question to the Right Hon. Prime Minister.

I will make my question very short. The Prime Minister did not answer the previous question. My question is the following.
In the counter proposal that has been forwarded to the Americans, is the Government of Canada asking for an extension of the October 5 deadline? In other words, are we asking the United States to give us more time to try to work out this deal, or are we finally going to cut bait and say that the deal is no good and we should get out?

First, Mr. Speaker, we have not forwarded a counter proposal to the Americans. Second, we are not asking for an extension, and third, you do not have to worry about my shoes because we will put the boots to you.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, according to a publication from the Prime Minister's former press secretary, he has already tried and failed.
Oh, oh!

We will wait for the publication of the book.
I want to return to the issue at hand. The Prime Minister said that we did not make a counter proposal, but in Question Period today he said, " but we are waiting for an American response". What is he waiting for a response to if he did not make a counter proposal? Why is it that even the Americans are confused? The spokesman for the trade negotiator's office says, "I do not know what this means." Is it consultation or negotiation? That is the same question Canadians are asking. What is the Government trying to do, is it consulting, negotiating or grovelling on its knees?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend says the Americans are confused. Perhaps that is the case. The Americans we have been speaking with on behalf of the Government of Canada, Secretary Baker and Ambassador Yeutter, are certainly not confused. They know the position of the Government of Canada. It has been clearly expressed by the Minister of Finance and the Minister for International Trade and it presumably is in the process of being considered by the American Government at which appropriate time I suppose there will be a response. However, they also know and have known from the very beginning that if the Government of Canada deems that matters are not acceptable, there shall be no deal. We have said this from the very beginning.

Point blank, will the Prime Minister tell us is the United States now seeking concessions on cultural industries and regional development and will this Government, despite its earlier promises, discuss these points?

subsubtopic: CITY OF MONTREAL- REQUEST FOR $25 MILLION GRANT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion, who is responsible for matters involving the greater Montreal area.
The Minister is fully aware that the Committee for Economic and Job Renewal in the East end of Montreal has published its recommendations, showing that despite the economic recovery, and contrary to what the Prime Minister stated earlier, the East end of Montreal is plagued with a very high, 12.4 per cent unemployment rate. In order to prevent the loss of thousands of jobs and to create new jobs, the Committee has put forward some 12 recommendations directly involving the Canadian government.
My question to the Minister is this: Would he be ready to inject $25 million into the setting up of a bureau to help restructuring and modernizing larger businesses, and to create a special fund for manpower training? Is the Minister ready to give a positive answer to that recommendation of the Pichette Committee?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: CITY OF MONTREAL- REQUEST FOR $25 MILLION GRANT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member mentioned, we have received the Pichette Committee report. That most interesting report clearly has required a lot of work. We are going to make an in-depth study of the recommendations and hopefully we will be in a position to respond to its special recommendations within the shortest time frame.

Mr. Speaker, the people in the East end of Montreal are just about sick and tired of this Government's numerous studies. subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF LAUNCHING OF CANADIAN SATELLITE

speakeroldname: Hon. Frank Oberle (Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF LAUNCHING OF CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, as we all know, marked the twenty-fifth anniversary of Canada's first venture into space with the launch of Alouette I, which was a scientific research satellite.
With the launch on September 29, 1962, of our first satellite, we positioned Canada to become a world leader in the peaceful occupation and the use of space. More important, we set the stage for us to build a space program which serves our national goals and our national aspirations.
Our space-based communications networks have drawn us together as a people and have played an important role in shaping our national character. As well, Canada's involvement in space will increasingly allow us to better understand and to manage our vast land and improve our custodial practices over our resources to protect and preserve our environment for the
benefit of future generations, perhaps through remote sensing and technologies developed by Canadian scientists and by Canadian engineers.
But while Canada has produced an amazing variety of sophisticated hardware of world-class distinction, the real story of this nation's space program has been the dedicated zeal of the pioneers who were associated with the programs, who for 25 years have had the vision, the courage and the foresight to compete with the very best in the world in the exploitation of a new frontier and to translate the knowledge we have gained into real benefits which are now enjoyed by all Canadians wherever they may live.
Our space efforts have helped us to bridge the vast distances of our land and have allowed even the most remote of our communities to become integrated into the mainstream of Canadian life. On behalf of the Government, therefore, I wish to pay tribute to the great efforts and the commitment of scientists, engineers, astronauts and, yes, even statesmen and politicians, who have built a solid foundation from which we have now launched a new effort.
Let us be inspired by our space pioneers to look ahead to the future prospects that await us. I am convinced the next 25 years will prove even more challenging and even more rewarding than our past endeavors. We have a proud history of accomplishment and a bright future in this silver anniversary year of Canada in space. I know that all Canadians would want to join us in celebrating this great Canadian success story.

subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF LAUNCHING OF CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF LAUNCHING OF CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join the Minister in commemmorating and celebrating Canada's 25 years in space. Canada's history in space is distinguished, not by glamour, prestige and dramatic adventure, but by a steadfast and continued commitment to the pre-eminent national need for reliable long range communications. As the Minister has said, it began September 29, 1962, with the NASA launch of Alouette. It was a Canadian made, designed and built satellite. It involved three years of workmanship, 20 years in manhours, and $3 million in federal financing. It was built to investigate the ionosphere and provided much valuable information over the years.
That was the beginning, but we continue to go forward. Indeed, Canada will participate with the United Kingdom, the United States in the RADARSAT satellite project which is scheduled to be launched in 1994. It is a remote sensing project that will monitor soil conditions, ship movements, and provide other information at a cost in total estimated today of $770 million, of which Canada will participate to the tune of $250 million. That will also include the participation of the provinces of Canada as well.
Canada, in the last number of years, has provided new pioneers for space, not only technicians and scientists, but these days astronauts. We now have six astronauts in this
September 30, 1987

country, all payload specialists, one of whom, it is worth noting, is a woman. Canada will participate in the U.S. space station at a cost of about $800 million over 15 years.
Many Canadians would welcome that development provided they can be assured, and there are still some concerns, of the use of such a program, provided that it is non-military and provided that the cost of Canada's $800 million worth of participation is not done at the expense of other research and development.
As much as I join the Minister in celebrating Canada's 25 years in space, I would be remiss if I did not remind the House, and indeed the Minister, as well as Canadians, that this Government had committed itself to increased R and D spending to 2.5 per cent of GNP in line with other major industrial nations. I know the Minister would like to see that happen. That was the commitment three years ago. The reality is an expenditure of roughly 1.3 per cent.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in his book Where I Stand committed himself to an expenditure increase of roughly 20 per cent in NRC. The reality is that there has been a reduction of nearly $400 million or a cumulative drop of 23 per cent. He promised an increase and we developed a drop of 23 per cent. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his Budget of February, 1986, announced an increase of $1 billion to federal granting agencies. The reality is that there will be a $335 million drop in base budgets of those same granting agencies.
Yes, Canada does have a proud tradition, Canada does have 25 years in space of which it can be proud and which it should celebrate. But those accomplishments were not only a reflection of the genious, the hard work and the dedication of the technicians and scientists of this country, they were a reflection of the commitment of the governments during those 25 years to see progress in Canada. That commitment can only continue, and the next 25 years can only be as bright when the Government of Canada continues the kind of financial commitment necessary for R and D in this country.

subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF LAUNCHING OF CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was a graduate student in the United States when the first satellite, Sputnik, was launched into space. It was traumatic for the nations of the west at the time, but as scientists we saw in the event the beginning of a new era for science. Subsequent developments fulfilled that hope. Working as a graduate student, it was with pride that 1 learned that 25 years ago my country, Canada, became the third country to orbit a satellite, Alouette I, thus establishing Canadian leadership in the peaceful exploitation of space.
It is meet that it has been through the use of extraterrestrial space that we have been able to enhance communications among our people, across the vast terrestial space of our land, and thus foster a nation more united.
Petitions
I wish to join the Minister in paying homage to the scientists and engineers who have, by their creativity, skill and knowledge, placed Canada among the front-ranks in the development of first-class space technology. It is technology that is not limited only to the exploitation of space but serves as well to enhancing the technological basis for industry as well as improving the lives of our citizens.
As we celebrate the twenty-fifth Anniversary of Alouette I, Canada has committed itself to the intensification of its efforts in space with its new $2 billion space program. In Radarsat we will be provided with extraterrestrial eyes to help us in managing our resources. In MSAT we will extend again our communications capacity, and in the development of the mobile servicing system we will expand our knowledge of and ability to exploit space.
As a scientist, I appreciate the significance of our involvement in space, but I also, as a scientist and as a citizen, must express my concerns. First, Canada must not allow its collaboration in space to become collaboration in advancing the destabilizing military policies of the United States respresented by the star wars initiative. We should commit ourselves to the more noble effort of establishing in space the monitoring systems that will provide confidence for the world in the security of future disarmament agreements.
Second, our research effort in space must not distort or allow us to forget our scientific efforts in other fields. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has noted, Canada remains minor league in its science effort and our space agency alone will not bring our general performance to the major league level.
While we are preoccupied with free trade as the basis for future industrial and economic development for Canada, we have shown virtually no commitment to the real basis for future growth, the expansion of knowledge. It is there, not elsewhere, that Canada's future lies.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seek leave, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 29, to move a motion for the adjournment of the House today on a matter of immediate and urgent concern, namely, the recent revelations regarding the Canadian Security Intelligence Service.
The series of information which has come out in recent days of CSIS infiltration of democratic organizations in Canada, including the labour movement, the peace movement, as well as legal political parties, give rise to grave concerns that must be dealt with on an urgent and emergency basis by the House.
In addition, clearly CSIS has dangerously mishandled its responsibilities in the area of counter-terrorism, including the Air-India disaster and the failure to take steps to provide for the protection of a visiting Punjabi cabinet minister.
In light of the series of events which have taken place and in light of the importance of an urgent debate on this situation, and, Mr. Speaker, in recognition of your earlier rulings under similar applications pursuant to Standing Order 29, I would hope there could be an emergency debate this evening on this serious and important question touching the civil liberties of all Canadians.
